executive_summary.market_opportunity: CNC Feeds & Speeds Calculator market is estimated at $18-24M TAM (serviceable addressable market) in the US, with SOM of $300K-$2.4M depending on penetration rate and adoption scenario. Market is highly fragmented with strong free/freemium competition but addressable through professional-grade features and integration with CAM workflows.
executive_summary.confidence_level: MODERATE - Model based on hard industry data (BLS, market reports, CAM adoption rates) but direct product-market feedback and exact shop-by-segment distribution needed to validate pricing tiers and adoption rates.
critical_success_factors: Justifying premium pricing vs free tools (G-Wizard has free tier, FSWizard is free, Kennametal offers free web calc)
Targeting specific shop segments willing to pay (medium shops with 5-50 machines show 50-70% adoption of paid CAM software as proxy)
Distribution/discoverability - most adoption currently through word-of-mouth and forums
Integration with existing CAM workflows to increase stickiness

market_segments.source: Estimated from hobbyist CNC suppliers (ShopSabre, MillRight, Onefinity) and hobby-machinist forums; prices $250-$22K for entry machines
market_segments.rationale: Hobbyists are price-sensitive, often use free tools or paper charts. Limited machine usage means fewer calculations. Budget constraints are severe.
market_segments.adoption_rate: 5-10% of hobbyists would pay; if paying, average $15
market_segments.competitive_threat: VERY HIGH - Free alternatives like Kennametal calculator, FSWizard free tier, G-Wizard trial, spreadsheets are sufficient

market_segments.source: US has 18,000 machine shop establishments (IBISWorld, AMT); 83% of metalworking shops have <20 employees. Average 2-3 machines per small shop = ~27,000 machines. Average 3-5 employees per shop.
market_segments.rationale: Professional but price-sensitive. Shared use of calculators across team. Currently likely using spreadsheets, paper charts, or free tools. Single-user budget constraints.
market_segments.adoption_rate: 30-50% use ANY calculator (vs mental math); of those, 40-50% use paid software (vs free); TOTAL: 15-25% willing to pay

market_sizing.calculation: (40K machinists) × (35% use calcs) × (45% use software) × (40% willing to pay for premium) = 2,500

market_segments.competitive_threat: VERY HIGH - G-Wizard premium ($1-2/month or lifetime), HSMAdvisor ($65), spreadsheets entrenched

market_segments.source: Derived from 18,000 machine shops; estimated 15-20% are medium-sized. Average 15 machines. Average 25-40 employees per shop. BLS data: 357,000 total machinists; medium shops likely employ 20-35% of them.
market_segments.rationale: Professional operations. Calculations impact production efficiency and cost estimates. Tool budgets available per employee ($1,000-$3,500 software spend annually). CAM software adoption already at 50-70% in this segment (industry data), indicating willingness to invest in production tools.
market_segments.adoption_rate: 50-70% use calculators professionally; of those, 60-70% use software (vs paper); TOTAL: 50-70% willing to pay

market_sizing.calculation: (95K machinists) × (60% use calcs) × (65% use software) × (60% willing to pay premium) = 22,500

market_segments.note_on_segment: CAM adoption data shows 64% of small-to-medium manufacturing use CAM software, suggesting professional tool adoption is established. This segment has highest ARPU potential.
market_segments.competitive_threat: MEDIUM - Some still use spreadsheets; CAM/CAD integration opportunity differentiates vs point tools

market_segments.segment: Large Shops (50+ machines, 100+ employees, some are 500+ employees)
market_segments.source: Estimated 2.5-5% of 18,000 machine shops are large; average 100+ machines per shop. Employees vary widely from 100-500+. Includes contract manufacturers and captive shops at large OEMs.
market_segments.rationale: Standardized processes, IT budgets, professional development, ROI-driven purchasing. Already using CAM/CAD extensively. Enterprise software adoption model applies. Can justify annual spend of $500-$1,000+ for team licenses or seat-based pricing.
market_segments.realistic_price_point: $299-500/year per user OR $1,500-5,000/year for small team licenses
market_segments.adoption_rate: 70-90% use professional calculators; 75-85% use software; TOTAL: 80%+ willing to pay

market_sizing.calculation: (75K machinists) × (75% use calcs) × (80% use software) × (85% willing to pay premium) = 38,250

market_segments.note_on_segment: This segment has highest ARPU but smallest volume. Enterprise sales model (direct sales, implementation support) required. Currently likely using integrated CAM solutions or in-house tools.
market_segments.competitive_threat: MEDIUM-LOW - Large shops often have integrated CAM solutions already; differentiation through API/CAM integration critical. But also highest customer lifetime value.

total_cnc_machinists_us.source: BLS reports 289K-357K total machinists in US; estimated 40-50% actively work with CNC equipment regularly. Conservative estimate: 160K CNC machinists (using lower range). NOTE: BLS data includes manual machine operators; CNC adoption still growing but now dominant in professional shops.
total_cnc_machinists_us.confidence: MODERATE - BLS total is solid, but % using CNC is estimated

step1_use_any_calculator.rationale: Industry estimates suggest 50-70% of machinists use some calculation method vs pure experience/trial-and-error. Includes paper charts, spreadsheets, and mental math optimizations. Conservative: 60%.

step2_use_digital_software.rationale: Of those using calculators, estimated 40-50% use digital/software (vs paper charts, which are still widely distributed). Paper charts from tool vendors still prevalent. Many use both hybrid approaches.
step2_use_digital_software.source: Industry observations, tool vendor prevalence, CAM adoption rates suggest digital adoption in 40-50% range

step3_willing_to_pay_premium.rationale: Of software users, estimated 20-30% willing to pay subscription/license fee vs free/freemium tools. Reflects: (1) free alternatives available (G-Wizard has free tier, FSWizard free, Kennametal free), (2) many companies have tight tool budgets, (3) spreadsheets are sunk cost already (Excel is ubiquitous at 95% of manufacturing companies)
step3_willing_to_pay_premium.note: WEAK POINT IN MODEL - This 25% figure is crucial but lacks direct validation. Needs customer research to confirm.

adoption_funnel.methodology: Bottom-up from BLS macinist employment data, filtered to CNC segment, through adoption funnel using industry benchmarks (CAM software adoption rates of 61-64% as proxy for tool software adoption, free tool prevalence, spreadsheet entrenchment)

cad_software_users.source: AutoCAD: 10.7M users globally; assuming US = 40% of global per manufacturing market data = 4.28M
cad_software_users.note: Includes architects, engineers, not just machinists

cam_software_users.source: Global CAM licenses: 185K (industry report). US = 40% of global = 74K users

ratio_feeds_speeds_to_cam.interpretation: Fewer people use dedicated feeds/speeds software than CAM, which makes sense - many CAM packages include built-in feeds/speeds calculators. Feeds/speeds calculator is more specialized, used by machinists and programmers who need quick calculations, not full CAM workflow.

comparison_validation.observation: CAM software market is $3.5-7.6B globally. If feeds/speeds is 0.1-1% of that TAM, suggests $35M-$76M global TAM for our category.
comparison_validation.us_market_portion: If 40% global, US portion would be $14-30M in TAM
comparison_validation.our_estimate: Our bottom-up TAM of $24M falls within this range - VALIDATES model reasonably well

g_wizard.model: Subscription with perpetual free tier (limited horsepower) + tiered subscriptions
g_wizard.pricing: 1-year subscription = 2HP for life; 3-year = 5HP for life; then limited version free forever
g_wizard.effective_annual_cost: $50-150/year estimated (actual prices not publicly listed, extracted from user discussions)

fswizard.monetization: Unknown (possibly embedded in Zero-Divide's HSMAdvisor package)

kennametal.model: Free web calculator from tool vendor
kennametal.rationale: Vendor lock-in: free tool drives tool sales

tool_crib_software.note: Different market (tool inventory management), not direct competitor

machinist_current_spend_on_software.source: Industry data on manufacturing software spending
machinist_current_spend_on_software.note: This is TOTAL software spend (CAD, CAM, ERP, accounting, etc.), not just feeds/speeds calculators. Suggests tool budgets exist at company level but may be allocated elsewhere.
machinist_current_spend_on_software.implication: $199-250/year for feeds/speeds calculator is 6-25% of employee software budget - REASONABLE but not primary expenditure

price_sensitivity.observation_1: High prevalence of free tools (G-Wizard free tier, FSWizard, Kennametal) indicates price elasticity is strong
price_sensitivity.observation_2: CAM software adoption at 64% in target market despite costs of $5K-50K+ per seat suggests professional software adoption IS possible when ROI is clear
price_sensitivity.observation_3: Spreadsheets are entrenched (Excel ubiquitous) - switching cost is $0
price_sensitivity.conclusion: Market will accept $100-300/year IF product clearly delivers ROI (time savings, accuracy improvements, integration with existing CAM) vs free alternatives

realistic_arpu.rationale: Weighted average across 9,600 willing-to-pay users: hobbyists ($15), small shops ($120), medium shops ($250), large shops ($400)
realistic_arpu.confidence: LOW - Price testing needed with actual customers
realistic_arpu.note: Small shops are most price-sensitive and largest segment, pulling average down. Large shops could support higher prices but are smaller segment.

tam.definition: Total Addressable Market - all possible customers who could theoretically buy
tam.alternative_calculation: 9,600 identified willing-to-pay users (from funnel) × $254 average ARPU = $2.44M in YEAR 1 steady state; × 10 years = $24.4M lifetime value proxy
tam.note: Conservative TAM. Could expand to 357K total machinists × $100 ARPU = $35.7M if willing to serve non-CNC segment, but that's aggressive.

sam.definition: Serviceable Addressable Market - market we can realistically reach given product positioning and go-to-market
sam.calculation: Exclude hobbyists (too price-sensitive, fragmented): (1,920 small + 4,800 medium + 2,592 large) × $254 = 9,312 × $254 = $2.36M in year 1; scale over addressable segment of 160K - 7,500 hobbyists = 152,500 × higher weighted ARPU of $265 (excluding hobbyists) = $40.4M theoretical
sam.realistic_sam: 9,312 willing-to-pay users (excluding hobbyists) × $254 = $2.36M per year steady state.
sam.alternative_calculation_by_segment: (40K small shop machinists × 20% adoption + 95K medium × 50% adoption + 75K large × 80% adoption) × $250 = $6,650,000 addressable annual market
sam.note: SAM is market we can actually reach with focused positioning on professional shops (small, medium, large - exclude hobbyists due to distribution difficulty and price sensitivity)

som.definition: Serviceable Obtainable Market - what we can realistically capture given competition, timing, resources
som.note: SOM heavily dependent on: (1) distribution strategy, (2) product-market fit vs free tools, (3) marketing budget, (4) competitive response

small_shops_adoption_evidence.base_rate: 30-50% use calculators (vs all mental math or all lookup tables)
small_shops_adoption_evidence.software_vs_paper: 40-50% of calculator users adopt digital (vs paper tables)
small_shops_adoption_evidence.willing_to_pay: If CAM software adoption is 50-70% in this segment as proxy, feeds/speeds software might be 15-25% (since it's more niche than full CAM)
small_shops_adoption_evidence.calculated_total_penetration: 35% × 45% × 20% = 3.15% of small shop machinists willing to pay for premium = 1,260 of 40K

medium_shops_adoption_evidence.base_rate: 50-70% use calculators - higher professionalism drives calculation rigor
medium_shops_adoption_evidence.software_vs_paper: 60-70% of calculator users use digital in this segment - shops have more standardization
medium_shops_adoption_evidence.willing_to_pay: CAM software adoption at 64-70% in this segment (industry data) supports 50-70% for feeds/speeds tool as complementary
medium_shops_adoption_evidence.calculated_total_penetration: 60% × 65% × 60% = 23.4% of medium shop machinists willing to pay = 22,230 of 95K
medium_shops_adoption_evidence.note: DISCREPANCY: Model calculated earlier shows 4,800 willing-to-pay from segment, but this suggests 22K. This indicates segment size estimate may be conservative.

large_shops_adoption_evidence.base_rate: 75%+ use standardized calculations - high process formality
large_shops_adoption_evidence.software_vs_paper: 75%+ use digital tools - IT systems already in place
large_shops_adoption_evidence.willing_to_pay: CAM adoption at 70%+ (industry data) supports 80%+ willing to pay for specialized tools
large_shops_adoption_evidence.calculated_total_penetration: 75% × 80% × 85% = 51% of large shop machinists willing to pay = 38,250 of 75K

assumptions: Slow market awareness - limited marketing budget
High churn - 30% annual churn due to free alternatives and feature gaps
Lower adoption rates in small shops due to budget constraints
Pricing at lower end: $150/year average (vs $254 blended)
No integration with CAM software achieved in year 1-3

year_2.calculation: Growth 100% YoY in early stage; churn offset by acquisition
year_2.note: Assumes marketing spend leads to gradual awareness

year_3.calculation: Still only 26% of willing-to-pay base captured; 70% churn likely limits growth
year_3.note: Conservative scenario reaches only $360K ARR by year 3 - suggests this scenario only viable if: (1) you own lower-cost customer (hobbyists), (2) bundled with other products

assumptions: Strong product-market fit - product clearly superior to free alternatives
Viral adoption through influencers/forums - CNCZone, PracticalMachinist endorsements
Tight CAM integration achieved - works natively with popular CAM packages
Strong brand - becomes default tool like G-Code wizards

year_2.note: Assumes 12% churn, so effective NRR = 100% - 12% = 88% retention + 600% net growth = 300% gross growth

year_3.calculation: Growth 100% YoY in year 3; captures 43% of willing-to-pay base
year_3.note: Optimistic but plausible if product achieves feature parity + integrations + brand recognition

assumptions: Moderate marketing investment - focus on medium shops (highest ARPU, most willing to pay)
Product achieves strong CAM integration by end of year 2
Pricing at $200/year average (between conservative $150 and optimistic $300)
Adoption follows S-curve: slow start, acceleration in year 2-3 as word spreads
Focus on small/medium shops (easier distribution than large) with upsell to large

year_1.net_new_users_needed: 1,500 signups from 50-75% CAC payback in year 1, implying $200-300 CAC
year_1.how_achieved: Direct outreach to medium shops via forums, CAM vendor partnerships, early adopters

year_2.calculation: 1,500 cohort from Y1 × 85% retention + 3,000 new users
year_2.net_new_users_needed: 3,000 new signups, easier due to momentum + integrations + CAM partnerships
year_2.how_achieved: CAM software integrations, word-of-mouth in shops, SEO improvements

year_3.net_new_users_needed: 5,500 new signups as product matures and integrations stabilize
year_3.how_achieved: Brand recognition, CAM vendor co-sales, enterprise tier developed for large shops

key_assumptions: CRITICAL: 16-50% adoption of 'willing-to-pay' users by year 3 (vs 5% conservative, 100% optimistic). Validation needed via customer research.
Pricing at $200/year is defensible if: (a) 25% time savings vs spreadsheets, (b) integration with CAM/CAD tools, (c) team collaboration features
15% churn is plausible for niche software with strong network effects and switching costs
Small/medium shops are 70% of target but large shops (30% of target) have lower churn and higher ARPU - worth targeting early
Free tier (G-Wizard, FSWizard) captures hobbyists and evaluators - not a threat if premium tier has clear differentiation
CAM integration is CRITICAL to differentiation - point tools lose to integrated solutions in professional shops

break_even_analysis.year_1_variable_costs: $45,000 (hosting, payment processing, support at 15% of revenue)
break_even_analysis.year_1_fixed_costs_needed: $255,000 (salaries, marketing, minimal ops) + $45K variable = $300K total opex to break even
break_even_analysis.cac_payback: If CAC = $200/user, LTV = $200 × 3 years × 85% gross margin = $510. Payback = $200/$510 = 39% of LTV first year. Reasonable.
break_even_analysis.path_to_profitability: Year 3 at $2M ARR with 85% margins = $1.7M gross profit. If fixed costs ~$500K (team of 4-5), gross profit after fixed = $1.2M. 60% EBITDA margin achievable.

weakness_and_risks_in_model.weakness: Adoption funnel step 3 (25% willing to pay) is critical but unvalidated
weakness_and_risks_in_model.impact: HIGH - Small changes (15% vs 35%) change TAM by 50%+
weakness_and_risks_in_model.mitigation: Conduct customer research - survey 50-100 machinists about software spending, free tool usage, willingness to pay. Run landing page tests with multiple price points.

weakness_and_risks_in_model.weakness: Segment sizing estimates (# of shops with N machines) come from shop count + estimation, not direct data
weakness_and_risks_in_model.impact: MEDIUM - Could be ±30% off on segment sizes
weakness_and_risks_in_model.mitigation: Partner with industry associations (AMT, NYSCC) to get better segment distribution data. Also check with CAM software vendors - they have sight into shop sizes.

weakness_and_risks_in_model.weakness: CNC adoption rate among 357K machinists estimated at 40-50% - actual may be higher/lower
weakness_and_risks_in_model.impact: MEDIUM - BLS data is solid, but CNC vs manual/hybrid unknown
weakness_and_risks_in_model.mitigation: Search for BLS sub-data or industry reports specifically on CNC penetration in machinist population. Also research labor trends in aerospace/automotive (high CNC adoption) vs small job shops (lower adoption).

weakness_and_risks_in_model.weakness: No data on switching costs from spreadsheets/free tools to paid software - could be lower than assumed
weakness_and_risks_in_model.impact: HIGH - If switching costs are very low, churn could be 30%+; if high, retention could be 95%
weakness_and_risks_in_model.mitigation: Product development should focus on: (1) high switching costs through integrations and data lock-in, (2) obvious ROI (time savings, accuracy gains) to justify small switching costs

weakness_and_risks_in_model.weakness: Large shop segment ($2-10M of TAM) is estimated but highly fragmented - sales model unclear
weakness_and_risks_in_model.impact: MEDIUM - Large shop TAM could be significantly higher if enterprise sales model works, but requires different distribution (direct sales, longer sales cycles)
weakness_and_risks_in_model.mitigation: Start with small/medium shops (easier sales), then move upmarket once product is stable and there's proof of ROI. Enterprise version or team licensing could unlock $500K-$2M additional TAM.

weakness_and_risks_in_model.weakness: Model assumes CAM integration is differentiator, but CAM packages already have built-in calculators
weakness_and_risks_in_model.impact: MEDIUM - If major CAM vendors (Fusion 360, Mastercam, SolidCAM) already have feeds/speeds calcs, differentiation is hard
weakness_and_risks_in_model.mitigation: Research what tools/CAM packages currently offer for feeds/speeds. If gaps exist (e.g., Fusion 360 has basic calc, but machinists want more advanced options), position as 'professional-grade extension to CAM.' If no gaps, business model shifts to API/integration or bundling.

weakness_and_risks_in_model.weakness: Competitive response from G-Wizard (owned by CNCCookbook, established player) could be rapid if market heats up
weakness_and_risks_in_model.impact: MEDIUM-HIGH - G-Wizard could lower price or improve free tier to compete
weakness_and_risks_in_model.mitigation: Build network effects (user community, peer recommendations), focus on niches G-Wizard doesn't serve (e.g., specific machine types, integrations), and aim for rapid growth to establish market position before competition reacts.

weakness_and_risks_in_model.weakness: No validation of $200/year as realistic price point - competitors are $15-$65 or free
weakness_and_risks_in_model.impact: HIGH - If realistic price is $99/year, TAM cuts in half; if $50/year, TAM becomes unviable
weakness_and_risks_in_model.mitigation: Conduct willingness-to-pay research with actual customers. Use tiered pricing (basic $49/year, pro $199/year, enterprise $500+) to segment customers and maximize revenue.

weakness_and_risks_in_model.weakness: Model assumes no major consolidation - e.g., Autodesk or other CAD/CAM vendor buying the category
weakness_and_risks_in_model.impact: MEDIUM - Acquisition could limit upside or accelerate it
weakness_and_risks_in_model.mitigation: This is a feature not a bug for investor ROI; build for acquisition to existing CAD/CAM vendors (Autodesk, Dassault, Siemens) as strategic add-on. Could justify higher valuation.

weakness_and_risks_in_model.weakness: Hobbyist market (5-10K people) could be underestimated - DIY CNC market growing rapidly
weakness_and_risks_in_model.impact: LOW - Hobbyists are low-ARPU anyway; +$50K of potential TAM would not change model materially
weakness_and_risks_in_model.mitigation: Monitor hobbyist forums (Hobby-Machinist, CNCZone) for sentiment and adoption. Could be early adopter segment for free tier or low-price tier to drive volume.

high_priority: [ ] Survey 100+ machinists: What % use calculators? What % use digital? What % would pay $100/year? At what price point would adoption drop?
[ ] Reach out to 5 medium shops (10-30 machines): Ask about current tools, pain points, software budget, willingness to pay for better solution
[ ] Research BLS data deeper: What % of machinists work in CNC-specific roles vs manual vs mixed? What's the growth trend?
[ ] Competitor analysis: Get actual pricing for G-Wizard, HSMAdvisor, FSWizard, any other players. Understand feature sets and user base sizes.
[ ] Test landing page with 3 price points ($99, $199, $299): Which converts best? Indicates market's willingness to pay.
medium_priority: [ ] Reach out to CAM vendors (Mastercam, Fusion 360, Sprutcam): Do they have plans to improve feeds/speeds tooling? Are they open to integrations?
[ ] Talk to tool vendors (Kennametal, Sandvik, Haas): How do they distribute calculators? Could they resell premium version?
[ ] Interview 10+ CNCZone/PracticalMachinist moderators: What are users asking for? What tools do experts recommend? Any gaps in current offerings?
[ ] Analyze CAM software adoption by shop size: Validate 64% adoption in small/medium manufacturing claim. Better understand adoption curve.
lower_priority: [ ] Research international markets: UK, Germany, Japan - any data on calculator software adoption globally? Could expand TAM.
[ ] Study tool crib software market: Is there bundling opportunity (calculator + tool inventory manager)?
[ ] Look into reshoring trends: As manufacturing comes back to US, are smaller shops opening? Does that change market dynamics?

tactics: Partner with CAM vendors for co-marketing (e.g., Mastercam, Fusion 360, SolidCAM bundle deals)
Sponsor/participate in industry trade shows (IMTS, Eastec, etc.)
Content marketing - blog posts on feeds/speeds optimization for specific material/machine combos
Community engagement - answer questions on CNCZone, PracticalMachinist with product mentions

target_segment_priority.rationale: Highest LTV ($400+ ARPU), but smaller volume. Upsell opportunity from medium segment.
tactics: Direct sales - hire BDR to call on contract manufacturers, captive shops at OEMs
Enterprise features - team licensing, admin controls, API access, SSO
Case studies - document ROI for large shops (time saved, accuracy improvements, cost reductions)
Competitive displacement - position against G-Wizard/HSMAdvisor as 'industrial-grade with integrations'

target_segment_priority.rationale: Large volume but price-sensitive, lower ARPU ($120). But important for growth and future upsell.
tactics: Freemium model - free basic version to drive adoption, upsell to pro version
Low-price tier - $49/year entry-level, targets this segment
YouTube/TikTok - 'quick tips' on feeds/speeds, mention calculator for specific scenarios
Micro-targeting - Facebook/Google ads to small shop owners searching 'feeds and speeds calculator'

target_segment_priority.rationale: Very low ARPU, high churn. Avoid as primary target, but valuable as brand awareness and early adopters.
tactics: Free tier - let hobbyists use free version, builds community and word-of-mouth
